beats.vo: Hey champ, welcome back! It's so good to see you again.
beats.caption: Welcome back, champ!

beats.vo: Last time, you grew number patterns, like one, one, two, three, five. And with that, you finished all of Unit one. Wow!
beats.caption: Unit 1 · Numbers Computers Love · done!

beats.vo: Today, we start Unit two. It's called, Logic and Reasoning. That's a fancy way of saying, thinking clearly, like a detective.
beats.caption: Unit 2 · Logic & Reasoning

beats.vo: And chapter one is a game you're going to love. It's called, True or False?
beats.caption: Chapter 1 · True or False?

beats.vo: By the end, you'll check sentences like a real logic detective. Let's go!
beats.caption: Become a logic detective!

beats.vo: Meet Kabir. Kabir's class is playing a game with Miss Rao. Every child has two cards. A green card that says true, and a red card that says false.
beats.caption: Meet Kabir · a green TRUE card, a red FALSE card

beats.vo: Miss Rao says, the sun rises in the east. Up go all the green cards. True! Every morning, the sun comes up in the east.
beats.caption: "The sun rises in the east." → TRUE

beats.vo: Then she says, all birds can fly. Almost everyone holds up green. But Kabir holds up red!
beats.caption: "All birds can fly." Kabir holds up FALSE!

beats.vo: Hmm. Why would Kabir say false? Birds fly, don't they? What do you think?
beats.caption: Why did Kabir say FALSE? Think!

beats.vo: Keep that thought. We'll come back to Kabir's red card very soon.
beats.caption: Hold that thought…

beats.vo: Miss Rao's sentences are called statements. A statement is a sentence that tells something, and can be checked.
beats.caption: Statement = tells something you can check

beats.vo: When we check it, there are only two answers. True means it matches the facts. False means it does not match the facts.
beats.caption: TRUE = matches the facts · FALSE = doesn't

beats.vo: For example, a cat has four legs. Let's check. One, two, three, four. Yes! It matches, so it's true.
beats.caption: "A cat has four legs." Check… TRUE!

beats.vo: But careful! Not every sentence is a statement. Please close the door. What time is it? Wow! A week has seven days. Which one can you mark true or false? Think.
beats.caption: Which one can be TRUE or FALSE?

beats.vo: A week has seven days! You can count the days and check. So it's a statement, and it's true.
beats.caption: "A week has 7 days" → a statement, TRUE

beats.vo: And the others? Please close the door is a request. What time is it, is a question. And wow is just a happy shout. You can't mark those true or false.
beats.caption: Request · Question · Shout → not statements

beats.vo: Here's the most important rule of this game. There's no maybe. Every statement is either true, or false. Just like the switches in binary. On, or off. Never in between.
beats.caption: No maybe! Only TRUE or FALSE

beats.vo: Let's test one. Five plus three equals eight. Count the counters. Five, and three more. Six, seven, eight. True!
beats.caption: 5 + 3 = 8 → count it… TRUE

beats.vo: Now, five plus three equals nine. But we just counted eight, not nine. So it's false. One wrong number makes the whole sentence false.
beats.caption: 5 + 3 = 9 → it's 8, so FALSE

beats.vo: Ten is an odd number. Let's pair up ten counters. Five pairs, and nothing left over. So ten is even, and that statement is false.
beats.caption: "10 is odd" → 5 pairs, none left → FALSE

beats.vo: Quick round, detective! Three is bigger than eight. A square has three sides. Cricket is played with a bat. True, or false? Pause, and decide.
beats.caption: Quick round: true or false?

beats.vo: Three is bigger than eight? On the number line, three comes way before eight, so three is smaller. False!
beats.caption: 3 comes before 8 → smaller → FALSE

beats.vo: A square has three sides? Let's count. One, two, three, four. Four sides! False again.
beats.caption: A square has 4 sides → FALSE

beats.vo: Cricket is played with a bat? Of course! True.
beats.caption: Cricket is played with a bat → TRUE

beats.vo: Now, remember Kabir's red card? All birds can fly. Let's check. A parrot flies. A crow flies. A sparrow flies.
beats.caption: Remember Kabir? Parrot, crow, sparrow… fly!

beats.vo: But what about a penguin? A penguin is a bird. And a penguin cannot fly! It waddles, and swims instead.
beats.caption: A penguin is a bird that can't fly!

beats.vo: So just one penguin makes all birds can fly, false. That one example is called a counter-example. It breaks the statement.
beats.caption: One counter-example → "all" is FALSE

beats.vo: Watch out for words like all, and every. They must work every single time. Even one miss, and the statement is false. Smart thinking, Kabir!
beats.caption: "All" and "every" must work every time

beats.vo: Your turn, detective. All fruits are red. Which fruit proves that's false? An apple, a strawberry, a banana, or a cherry? Think.
beats.caption: "All fruits are red." Which fruit breaks it?

beats.vo: The banana! It's a fruit, and it's yellow, not red. The apple, strawberry and cherry are red, so they can't break the rule. One banana is enough!
beats.caption: Banana! A yellow fruit → FALSE

beats.vo: Here's a tricky one. Every number that ends in five is odd. True, or false? Think.
beats.caption: "Every number ending in 5 is odd." T or F?

beats.vo: Let's pair up. Five makes two pairs, with one left over. Fifteen makes seven pairs, with one left over. Twenty five makes twelve pairs, and one left over. True!
beats.caption: 5, 15, 25 → always one left over → TRUE

beats.vo: And here's why it always works. Tens always pair up perfectly. The five at the end makes two pairs, and leaves one alone. So every number ending in five is odd.
beats.caption: Tens pair up · the 5 leaves one alone

beats.vo: Now, here's why computers love this game. They check true or false questions all the time, to decide what to do next.
beats.caption: Computers check TRUE or FALSE to decide

beats.vo: A game says, if your score is more than ten, you win. Your score is twelve. Is that true, or false?
beats.caption: More than 10 wins. Score 12: true or false?

beats.vo: True! Twelve is more than ten, so you win! But if your score was seven, it's false, so you play again.
beats.caption: 12 → TRUE, you win! 7 → FALSE, play again

beats.vo: That true or false check is called a condition. You met it in coding, with if this, then that. Every game and app is full of them!
beats.caption: A true or false check in code = a condition

beats.vo: Okay champ, here's a practice check, just like the quiz.
beats.caption: Your turn: practice check

beats.vo: True or false? Every even number ends with zero, two, four, six, or eight. Try a few numbers on paper, and hunt for a counter-example. Pause, and think.
beats.caption: Every even number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8?

beats.vo: It's true! Fourteen ends in four. Twenty ends in zero. Thirty six ends in six. The tens always pair up, so only the last digit decides. And the even digits are zero, two, four, six, and eight. Brilliant!
beats.caption: TRUE! 14, 20, 36… no counter-example

beats.vo: Let's remember what we learned today. A statement is a sentence that's true, or false.
beats.caption: A statement is true or false

beats.vo: In this game, there's no maybe.
beats.caption: No "maybe" in this game

beats.vo: One counter-example, like a penguin, makes all false.
beats.caption: One counter-example makes "all" false

beats.vo: And code uses true or false to decide what to do.
beats.caption: Code uses true or false to decide

beats.vo: Chapter one of Unit two, done! You're a real logic detective now, champ.
beats.caption: Chapter 1 done!

beats.vo: Now let's see what you remember. Tap Finish, and try the quiz. You've got this!
beats.caption: Next: Quiz · Tap Finish
